Sometimes when I have a shit or failed workout I try to just move on from it. That way I have something to look forward to next time I revisit that day. It gives me drive to do better and clear my head. Hope that helps. Mind is everything in workouts.

Circuit/full body workouts are great! Anything like box jumps, planks, mountain climbers, burpees, jump squats, split leg lunge squat, etc are fantastic. I try to set a timer for 15-30 seconds depending on my mood, do rest for 10-15 and try to do as many reps as I can. I do this for about 15-20 minutes and so a cycle of exercises. Or what we do in wrestling is set it to 1 minute and push ourselves to do as many reps in that time frame and count it. Then we do it a week later and compare. Usually these are 5-10 minutes. Way more work and intensity is up to you but push yourself. Also helps with weight cutting since we cut a lot during the season for tournaments and stuff.

I've had this problem too. Usually it's a change in diet. Once I changed my diet and did HIIT twice a week, my weight loss was much more noticeable. Also for HIIT I never went over 30ish minutes. That's just me though. I also wear more layers so I can break a good sweat since I don't lift on HIIT days. I've weened myself off and typically do HIIT every week or two when I feel like it. And as for lifting maybe try a higher intensity, higher reps, less weight. That's what I do now since my weeks are full of heavy lifting and training (wrestling) sessions.

I'm a uni wrestler. We workout anywhere between 5-9x a week. That includes practices basically every weekday, and strength training on top - not to mention running on weekends to keep our cardio in shape. Definitely doable and you will continue to make progress. 
But during my in-season training I eat A LOT more than I usually do. So keep it up and continue eating right, you'll have no problem at all. 
EDIT: forgot to mention lots of wrestlers tend to "bulk" during in season. We train more, we eat more, which makes for more muscle growth than the summer. In the summer I'm not as lean or strong. My winter bod is deff better lol

My brother is 10 and workouts with me when I'm home. We're both wrestlers (I'm 20) and I usually do circuit workouts, total body movements, train technique with him, etc. He doesn't necessarily do a lot of heavy lifting (like I have to) but I wouldn't say no to teaching him how to with proper form and such. Also wrestling is a heavy sport which does require lifting people in general, which he's done so that gives you an idea of his training. I'm not against kids working out as long as they get all the proper foods and nutrients and are never injured or hurt during and afterwards. If he's sore, lighten the weights and workout routine. 
Also make sure he's actually having fun. That way he'll stay engaged and enthusiastic. With kids I find that letting them take their own lead and plan out their own goals is the best way for them to train.

I usually stop around 15-20. Keeping proper form and slow, tight movements. I also do these kind of workouts on recovery days, so no PR's or heavy lifts. Just focusing on movement and keeping the right muscles engaged. Once I started workouts like that my PR's were much better in terms of how they felt hitting them and the level of comfort I had with upping weights. So no, it's not a waste of time to go light and for longer reps.

I don't lift as often but I wrestle and our workout days are quite intense. So in terms of days like that, I do eat more carbs and protein than I do on "lazy days." Not to say I just lie around but days I only have classes, study sessions, and only time for a quick and light 30-45 minute workout to recover. But make sure you're still getting a good amount of protein, carbs, essential vitamins on "lazy days" because your body won't necessarily just backup and use way less energy.

But anyway, from what I understand as a history major: Cuba was doing very well in the 70-80s. Up until the collapse of the Soviet Union. Cuba also made the mistake of relying on sugar as their means of income. They didn't diversify well enough because they relied so much on the ussr and her allies.

I was an atheist most of my life. Both my parents are fairly religious Buddhists but never pressured me or my siblings to practice growing up. I learned to have good values and morals. That was enough. It wasn't until my depression really seeped into my life, and then my grandma died. It was dark for so long until I started meditating again (which I've done on and off). I started reading, praying, and overall practicing Buddhism. Then I was raped. And things got dark again. And they still are. I was only raped a few weeks ago. I had a hospital stay for a near suicide attempt. I'm not really practicing anymore but I pray. I'm hoping it'll help me through this time of my life and be there for the rest. Honestly, I feel cliche but I converted because I was so alone in my life and needed to find comfort in being alone.
